This feature fires on the little “label” tokens that kick off new segments or headings—short, content‐bearing words or abbreviations (nouns like people, forms, bias, book, navy; version numbers like 2; citation markers like F. and S.; suffixes like -s/-ing) that typically introduce a title, section, or legal reference.

This neuron is simply firing on “continuation” subword pieces—short BPE fragments that occur inside words (no preceding space), like isk- in Finnish yhteiskunnassa, orb- in phorbol, min- in plasminogen, fel- in Creutzfeldt, 样 in 样式, wh- in rawhide, etc.

explanations.explanation: This feature is a detector for semantically rich content words—especially main verbs, adjectives, and adverbs that carry the core action, state, or evaluative nuance of a sentence—across varied English contexts.

This neuron fires on the structural markers that introduce or separate blocks and identifiers in technical text—above all the “.” token when it appears in filenames, version numbers, package/namespace paths, XML tags, URLs, etc., and (at higher strength) on the section-heading keywords or tool names (e.g. source, reference, APP, Concuerror, List) that kick off those blocks.

This feature fires on standardized header‐field tokens in formal documents—i.e. the labels and markers (Date, Filed, Rule, HEAD/ER, 107, etc.) used to introduce metadata in license headers, court filings, email headers, and similar top-of-document sections.
This feature detects the sentence-final period (full stop) marking an end-of-sentence boundary.

This neuron fires on the “boilerplate” or meta-text that surrounds main content—things like section headers, bylines/captions, site-navigation or registration prompts, calls-to-action, disclaimers and other framing labels (e.g. “Reuters,” “Welcome to…,” “Subscribe now,” “Editor’s Note,” “Programming: This forum is…,” etc.).

This feature is a “title‐headline” detector: it lights up on the initial, often capitalized token (or its closing punctuation) of standalone headings and titles (across abstracts, news blurbs, recipe names, etc.), marking the start (or end) of a document or section header.

This feature fires on the little “label” characters that introduce structured markers in technical/academic text—chiefly the single‐letter prefixes in bracketed citations (e.g. the “b” in [@b6], “R” in (R5–8), etc.) and analogous single‐letter tokens in section IDs or HTML/Markdown tags (e.g. `<a>`, `<li>`, code fences). It thus abstracts the signalling of bibliographic or structural markers in scientific and technical documents.

This feature fires on the “.” token whenever it’s acting as a hard boundary or delimiter—whether as a sentence-final full stop (titles, headings, blog snippets), or as the dot that separates parts of structured strings (URLs/.com, package paths, version numbers, abbreviations like ASP.NET).

explanations.explanation: This neuron lights up on the little “relation markers” in journalese—prepositions and particles (often in phrasal verbs) that introduce a topic, object or complement (e.g. about, on/over, in mind, take on, brought about, come up with, as to, etc.).

This feature fires on the “meat” of long, domain-specific names or terms—i.e. the subword pieces (BPE tokens) that continue through multi-token proper nouns or technical compounds (disease names, gene prefixes, file‐ or product-names, camel-cased identifiers, etc.). It flags when you’re in the heart of a specialized entity rather than ordinary language.
This neuron just lights up on the hyphen/dash token—especially when it’s used to link things in an “X-and-Y” or similar compound (e.g. tried-and-true, cat-and-mouse, one-and-a-half, bib-0019, etc.).

This feature flags the key topic labels or principal action words that head sections in technical prose—whether titles or major clauses—such as library names (“Buffers”), configuration commands (“Build”), metrics (“Total Cost”) or the core gerund/past-participial verbs that introduce functional statements (“utilizing,” “governed,” “distributed”).
This feature fires on parenthesized uppercase abbreviations—i.e. the moment a document introduces an acronym (often in parentheses) immediately after its spelled‐out name.
This neuron fires on the terminal period that ends standalone headings or titles—i.e. the “.” marking the close of a label-like phrase across domains.

explanations.explanation: This feature seems to mark the little “labels” that introduce parts of a list or outline—e.g. Roman‐numeral (i, ii, iii), numeric (1, 2, 3), or lettered (a, b, c) item markers (and their enclosing punctuation) in scientific, technical, or code‐like texts.

This neuron is a boundary‐detector: it spikes on the “dot” token (whether a sentence-final period, an abbreviation marker like “No.”/“Dr.”/“Mo.,” or a version-number separator) and on the very first word of a new sentence or heading (e.g. “Currently,” “Complete,” “Yesterday,” “This,” etc.). In effect it marks sentence‐ or section‐breaks in running text.

This feature is essentially a sub‐token/boundary detector: it spikes on the first piece of a new semantic unit—whether that’s the start of a CamelCase segment or morpheme (“Bra” in JetBrains, “raz” in tetrazolium, “rop” in neutropenia, “Enter,” “Explorer”) or the punctuation that splits key/value or property definitions (the “=”, “:=”, “:=”/”” tokens in config, XML/HTML, file‐format specs).

This feature is essentially a “boundary” detector – it lights up on sentence‐ or section‐ending punctuation (the final full stop or break after a heading), signaling the end of one textual unit and the start of the next.

This neuron fires on the little “glue” words and symbols that link names to their provenance or category membership—tokens like “from,” “of,” “an”/“and,” “&,” etc., as they appear in proper-noun phrases (People from X, Hall of Fame, B&N, S&W, New York Post, airport or place names, scientific site names, etc.). It’s essentially a relational/connective-phrase detector in entity‐description contexts.

Here’s a one‐line, abstract description for each feature based on the starred tokens and their contexts:

• Ama (“Ama­zing…”): a high-energy intensifier marking enthusiastic praise or wonder.  
• Generally (“Generally speaking,…” / “Generally, a pneumatic…”): a framing cue introducing a broad or typical statement.  
• Zoom (“Zoom in to use Hail Finder…”): a UI/navigation prompt telling the user to magnify or focus on content.  
• Currently (“Currently 34 Lyf Mobile Phones…” / “Currently unavailable”): a status marker situating information in the present moment.  
• Everyone (“Everyone, not least his…” / “Everyone in journalism knows…” / “Everyone loves…”): a universal quantifier used to introduce a claim about all or most people.  
• Look (“Look of the Day” / “Look how proud…”): an attention‐getter directing the reader’s gaze or focus.  
• Recently (“Recently the eccentric…” / “Recently, heavyweight contender…” / “Recently, there have been…”): a temporal cue signaling that what follows happened in the near past.  
• Sure (“Sure, money talks.” / “Surely you do not think…”): a discourse hedge or concession marker softening or qualifying what follows.  
• Interest (“Interesting. Did he pick that…”): a reaction token expressing mild evaluation or curiosity before further commentary.

This neuron lights up on approximate‐quantity phrases—words like “dozens,” “hundreds,” “thousands,” “a number of,” etc.—especially when they introduce lists or scale in informational or news‐style contexts.

This feature is a detector for end‐of‐word subtoken fragments—i.e. the common suffix pieces (morphological endings like “-ing”, “-ed”, “-ize”, numeric tails, or the tail segment of CamelCase/snake_case identifiers) that occur at the end of identifiers or words.
This feature is a character‐n‐gram detector that fires on common word‐final letter sequences—i.e. it recognizes suffix‐like endings across diverse tokens.
This feature detects sentence-final periods—i.e. the full-stop marking the end of a declarative sentence in formal/technical prose.

explanations.explanation: This neuron flags tokens that kick off section or list headings—e.g. titles, numbered or bulleted item labels, major subhead markers and the first word of a new paragraph or heading.

This feature fires on the trailing “0” in dotted version strings (e.g. “1.0,” “2.0,” “4.0”) as they appear in structured technical contexts—XML configs, license headers, code comments—i.e. the zero‐valued minor/patch component of software or spec version numbers.

This feature detects the little punctuation tokens (dots, hyphens, apostrophes, etc.) that glue together multi-part codes and names—things like U·S· (abbreviations), L-T4 (drug/chemical prefixes), 2×80×9 (dimensional specs), O’Reilly (names), and similar hyphenated or dot-separated identifiers.

This neuron consistently lights up on the main noun of a noun phrase when that noun names a significant concept, event or entity—whether an abstract quality (intelligence, animosity, enthusiasm), a historical or organizational label (World War II, Lakers, NBA Finals), or a concrete count noun in a descriptive context (bins). It is effectively a “head‐noun detector” for semantically important English terms.

The feature is picking out “declaration/-binding” markers in code.  Whenever you see a storage-class or import/namespace specifier (const, final, namespace, the “{” of a destructuring import, the “\” in a PHP use, the “(” of a for, etc.), this feature lights up to flag that you’re at the start of a declaration or import binding.

This feature consistently lights up on single-word noun tokens used as labels or category names—standalone object or class identifiers (e.g. “slant,” “diamond,” “Ice,” “Tag,” “stripe,” “HDL,” “boxing,” “Mail,” “Bed,” “Jet,” “knife,” “Drag,” “lift,” “sword,” “BOX,” etc.) across varied contexts.
This feature detects four‐digit year tokens (e.g. “1992,” “2018”) used as temporal markers in formal texts—copyright notices, license headers, and legal filing/decision dates.

This neuron appears to fire on the “head” words of domain-specific concepts and abstract properties—i.e. tokens that name a key idea, category or relation (whether a proper name like Dixit, Unity or Kingdom; a Greek-letter measure like α; a property adjective like elastic, noble or singular; or a relational/nominal term like linkage, affinity, relationship, signature, credibility, constitutive, –uity, etc.). In short, it flags the conceptual labels or vocabulary kernels that introduce important technical or categorical notions across diverse fields.
